Important Limitations of this Backtest:
(1) Look-ahead bias — uses current financials as screening criteria for all historical years. Real point-in-time data would differ; results are likely optimistic.
(2) Survivorship bias — universe contains only current S&P 500 constituents. Companies removed since 2021 (failed, merged, delisted) are excluded.
(3) Single-day pricing — entry/exit on one date per year, no slippage or bid-ask spread.
(4) No transaction costs — commissions and taxes are not modelled.
Treat results as directional indicators of strategy quality, not as reliable future predictions.
▶ ⚙ How the Engine Works — Methodology 6 sections  ·  data pipeline, valuation models, 4 screens, backtest
Every sub-section below is also collapsible. All descriptions reflect what is actually running in the code — no planned features included.
▶ DB 1  —  Data Pipeline & Caching

The S&P 500 universe (503 tickers) is fetched live by scraping Wikipedia on every run. Financial data is pulled from Yahoo Finance via yfinance: current price, balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement (3–5 years of history), beta, dividends, shares outstanding, and 52-week range. Every ticker goes through a retry loop with exponential backoff (3 attempts, ~1s delay doubling). Fetching runs concurrently via ThreadPoolExecutor with a configurable number of workers.

What is cachedTTL policy
Prices, multiples, financialsTTL = 0 — always re-fetched fresh from Yahoo Finance on every run. Stale prices would produce incorrect valuations.
Historical price seriesTTL = 1 day — historical closes never change; one-day cache avoids redundant downloads during the backtest.
Cache storageSingle DuckDB file at data/cache.duckdb. Thread-safe writes via a lock. A full re-run from a warm cache completes in ~8 seconds.

Limitation: Yahoo Finance is an unofficial, undocumented data source. Some tickers may return incomplete or stale data; the engine marks those as INSUFFICIENT_DATA and skips them gracefully.

▶ IV 2  —  Valuation Models — How Intrinsic Value is Computed

Every company gets a per-share intrinsic value from two independent DCF models (or DDM for financial-sector companies). The final value is their arithmetic average. Margin of Safety = (Intrinsic − Price) / Intrinsic × 100.

ModelLogicUsed when
DCF — Gordon Growth Model (GGM) 3–5 year average FCF projected 10 years at a per-company growth rate g = ROE × Retention Ratio (capped at WACC − 1%, floored at 1%). Terminal value via perpetuity: TV = FCFₙ × (1+g) / (WACC − g). Everything discounted at the per-company WACC. Result divided by diluted shares outstanding. All non-financial sectors where FCF > 0
DCF — Exit Multiple Average EBITDA projected 10 years at the same growth rate, multiplied by a 12× EV/EBITDA exit multiple at year 10, net debt subtracted, result discounted at WACC, divided by shares. Acts as a cross-check on GGM — if both agree, conviction is higher. All non-financial sectors where EBITDA > 0
DDM — Dividend Discount Gordon growth formula: P = D₁ / (r − g) where D₁ = next-year dividend, r = WACC, g = sustainable dividend growth. Used because FCF and EBITDA from cash flow statements are unreliable for banks and insurers (capital tied up in regulatory reserves is not “free”). Financial Services & Insurance sectors only
Dynamic WACC Per-company: WACC = Ke × (E/V) + Kd × (1−t) × (D/V). Ke = risk-free rate (US 10Y ^TNX, live) + beta × 5.5% equity risk premium. Kd = interest expense / total debt. Fallback to 10% if data is missing. All models above

Limitations: DCF is inherently sensitive to the growth rate assumption — a 1pp change in g can move intrinsic value by 15–30%. FCF figures from yfinance use the reported statement; capitalised R&D or leases may distort results. The 12× exit multiple is fixed; cyclical sectors (Energy, Basic Materials) may warrant a lower multiple at trough.

▶ QS 3  —  Quality Scores — Piotroski, Altman Z, ROIC, Composite
ScoreHow it is calculatedThresholds & flags
Piotroski F-Score 9 binary (0/1) accounting signals summed to a score 0–9. Four profitability signals (positive ROA, positive operating cash flow, improving ROA YoY, CFO > Net Income); three leverage/liquidity signals (falling long-term debt ratio, improving current ratio, no new share dilution); two efficiency signals (improving gross margin, improving asset turnover). Signals F6 and F7 are computed where data allows; otherwise capped at 7. ≥ 7 strong 4–6 stable ≤ 3 weak
Altman Z-Score Z = 1.2×X₁ + 1.4×X₂ + 3.3×X₃ + 0.6×X₄ + 1.0×X₅ (Working Capital/TA, Retained Earnings/TA, EBIT/TA, Market Cap/Total Debt, Revenue/TA). Threshold calibrated at 1.0 instead of the textbook 1.81 to avoid over-excluding media and telecom companies with large intangible asset bases whose tangible asset ratios are structurally lower. ≥ 3.0 safe 1.0–2.99 grey zone < 1.0 distress
ROIC ROIC = NOPAT / Invested Capital, where NOPAT = Operating Income × (1 − tax rate) and Invested Capital = Total Equity + Total Debt − Cash & Equivalents. Measures how efficiently the business converts capital into profit regardless of financing structure. ≥ 15% moat 10–14% good < 10% weak
Composite Score (0–100) Weighted blend of four normalised signals:
 • Margin of Safety % — 40% weight
 • Piotroski F-Score — 25% weight
 • ROIC — 25% weight
 • 52-week Position (inverted: lower = better) — 10% weight
Used internally for ranking and as the 30% quality component of ProfileFit. 		—
▶ DV 4A  —  Screen: Deep Value — the tightest six-filter pass

Philosophy: Benjamin Graham–style deep discount. A company must pass all six criteria simultaneously to receive a strict PASS. No single strong metric compensates for a failure in another. Designed to find statistically cheap stocks where the price alone offers a wide margin of safety.

CriterionThresholdRationale
P/E ratio≤ 15×Below long-run S&P 500 average (∼22×). At ≤15× the market prices in meaningful pessimism about earnings.
P/B ratio≤ 1.5×Near or below book value. Classic Graham criterion: paying ≤1.5× assets provides downside protection.
EV/EBITDA≤ 8×An acquirer could recover the full enterprise value from operating profit in ≤8 years — historically cheap.
P/FCF≤ 15×Free cash flow yield ≥6.7%. Real cash generation, not accounting earnings.
Net Debt / EBITDA≤ 2.5×Conservative leverage. Debt repayable from operating profit in ≤2.5 years.
Margin of Safety≥ 20%DCF intrinsic value at least 20% above current price.
Piotroski F-Score≥ 4Minimum accounting quality check. Prevents buying deteriorating businesses that happen to look statistically cheap.
Altman Z < 1.0 excludedAuto-excludeCompanies in real financial distress are removed even if multiples look cheap.

Sorted by: Margin of Safety % (descending). Typical pass rate: 1–5 companies from 503 tickers — the strictest screen in the system. Known limitation: Very cheap multiples in cyclical sectors (Energy, Materials) may reflect a trough in the cycle, not a permanent discount; combine with sector context.

▶ BQ 4B  —  Screen: Buffett Quality — wide-moat business at a fair price

Philosophy: “It’s far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.” Focuses on quality first: strong return on invested capital, improving accounting fundamentals, low debt, and a DCF-confirmed discount. Multiples are more relaxed than Deep Value because the quality premium is justified.

CriterionThresholdRationale
P/E ratio≤ 25×Allows paying a modest quality premium above the market average.
P/B ratio≤ 4×High-ROIC businesses trade above book; 4× still filters out the most expensive growth names.
EV/EBITDA≤ 15×Enterprise value check; still materially below the top quintile of the S&P 500.
P/FCF≤ 25×FCF yield ≥4%. Ensures real cash generation even for quality businesses.
Net Debt / EBITDA≤ 1.5×Stricter than Deep Value — Buffett-style businesses should not need excessive leverage to generate returns.
Margin of Safety≥ 15%Slightly relaxed vs Deep Value; quality businesses rarely trade at a 20%+ discount.
Piotroski F-Score≥ 5Above-average accounting quality. Rising profitability and falling leverage.
ROIC≥ 10%Must exceed typical cost of capital — the defining criterion separating Buffett-style from pure value.

Sorted by: Margin of Safety % (descending). Typical pass rate: 2–10 companies. Known limitation: ROIC data from yfinance may be missing for recent IPOs or companies undergoing restructuring; those are scored 0 on the ROIC criterion but not excluded.

▶ FCF 4C  —  Screen: High FCF Yield — maximum cash generation

Philosophy: Free cash flow is the most honest measure of a company’s earning power because it is harder to manipulate than net income (no non-cash charges, no accruals). This screen finds companies where the cash yield on the market price is exceptionally high — meaning the business is generating so much cash that even at a conservative DCF valuation it still looks cheap. Multiples filters are intentionally broad to avoid excluding asset-light or high-depreciation businesses that score well on FCF.

CriterionThresholdRationale
P/FCF≤ 12×The core criterion. FCF yield ≥8.3% — an exceptional cash return at any interest rate environment.
Margin of Safety≥ 10%Minimum DCF confirmation that the cash yield is not just a one-year artefact.
P/E ratio≤ 30×Guardrail only — broad enough not to exclude high-depreciation or capital-intensive companies.
EV/EBITDA≤ 20×Broad ceiling to catch companies with unusual capital structures.
Net Debt / EBITDA≤ 3.0×Slightly more lenient than other screens because strong FCF can service higher debt levels.

Sorted by: Margin of Safety % (descending). Typical pass rate: 8–20 companies. Known limitation: A single year of elevated FCF (asset sale, working capital release) can produce a deceptively low P/FCF. The engine uses a 3–5 year FCF average in the DCF, but the P/FCF multiple is based on trailing twelve months reported FCF. Always cross-check with the FCF trend over 3+ years.

▶ QV 4D  —  Screen: Quality Value — financially healthy at a discount

Philosophy: A balanced blend of quality and price discipline. The screen requires a demonstrably healthy balance sheet (Altman Z ≥ 1.0), above-average capital efficiency (ROIC ≥ 10%), improving fundamentals (Piotroski ≥ 5) and a clear DCF discount. It avoids the “too cheap for a reason” problem by requiring quality, and avoids overpaying by requiring a margin of safety. Results are sorted by Composite Score (not just MoS) to surface the best risk-adjusted picks.

CriterionThresholdRationale
P/E ratio≤ 25×Moderate multiple ceiling. Allows quality businesses that trade above deep-value levels.
P/B ratio≤ 4×Same as Buffett Quality — permits intangible-rich businesses.
EV/EBITDA≤ 15×Enterprise value discipline; below the top third of the S&P 500 by this metric.
P/FCF≤ 20×FCF yield ≥5%. Meaningful but not extreme cash yield required.
Net Debt / EBITDA≤ 2.5×Moderate leverage ceiling to keep balance sheet risk manageable.
Margin of Safety≥ 15%DCF discount of at least 15% required to confirm valuation, not just quality.
Piotroski F-Score≥ 5Above-average accounting quality. Fundamentals improving, not deteriorating.
ROIC≥ 10%Capital efficiency above cost of capital. Confirms the business earns real returns.
Altman Z < 1.0 excludedAuto-excludeFinancial distress guard. Unlike Deep Value, Quality Value explicitly removes distressed names even if all other criteria pass.

Sorted by: Composite Score (descending) — not raw MoS%. This surfaces the best-balanced companies rather than just the most deeply discounted. Typical pass rate: 2–8 companies.

▶ PF 5  —  ProfileFit Score & Full-Universe Ranking

Rather than a binary pass/fail, every company receives a ProfileFit Score (0–100) per profile. This allows ranking all 503 companies, not just the handful that strictly pass. Companies that almost pass are visible and comparable to those that do pass.

ComponentWeightHow it is computed
Criterion proximity score 70% For each threshold in the profile, a score 0–1 is given: 1.0 = at or better than threshold; partial credit for being close (e.g. if threshold is P/E ≤15 and actual P/E is 20, score = 15/20 = 0.75). The average across all profile criteria gives the proximity score.
Composite Score 30% The 0–100 quality-adjusted ranking score described in section 3.

PASS = meets every criterion in the profile strictly.
NEAR = misses one or more criteria but still has a meaningful ProfileFit score.
TRAP = Value Trap flag active: Net Debt/EBITDA > 3.5× or all FCF years are negative.
INSUFFICIENT_DATA = fewer than 2 financial data points available; always placed last.

The Top Overall section at the top of the report aggregates ProfileFit scores across all four profiles using a weighted average (Deep Value ×1.3, Buffett Quality ×1.2, Quality Value ×1.1, FCF Yield ×1.0) to produce a single cross-profile ranking.

▶ BT 6  —  Walk-Forward Backtest vs S&P 500

Annual simulation of the Deep Value screen applied to historical data. Top-N picks bought on the first trading day of each year, held for exactly one year, sold on the first trading day of the following year. Portfolio is equal-weighted. Benchmark is ^GSPC (S&P 500 total price return).

MetricHow it is computed
CAGRCompound Annual Growth Rate of a $1 investment over the full backtest period.
Sharpe Ratio(Mean annual return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation of annual returns. Risk-free rate = US 10Y yield at the time.
Sortino RatioSame as Sharpe but uses only downside deviation in the denominator. Penalises losses more than gains.
Max DrawdownLargest peak-to-trough loss of the cumulative portfolio value across all years.
Win RatePercentage of individual stock picks that outperformed the S&P 500 in their holding year.
Excess ReturnPortfolio return minus S&P 500 return for each year, and CAGR difference over the full period.
Critical limitations — read before drawing conclusions:
  • Look-ahead bias: screening criteria use current financial data for all historical years. A company that passes the screen today may not have passed in 2018 with its then-current financials. Results are optimistic.
  • Survivorship bias: universe = current S&P 500 constituents only. Companies that failed, were acquired, or were removed from the index since the start year are absent. This overstates historical returns.
  • Single entry/exit date: one buy and one sell date per year, no dollar-cost averaging, no intra-year rebalancing.
  • No costs: commissions, bid-ask spread, market impact, taxes, and short-selling costs are not modelled.
  • Interpretation: treat as a directional indicator of whether the strategy has historically identified above-average companies — not as a reliable forecast of future returns.
